claim: Cre expression faithfully reports Chat expression in cerebral cortex with 97% of Chat+ neurons expressing Cre and 100% of Cre+ neurons expressing Chat.
source: We confirmed that Cre expression faithfully reports Chat expression in cerebral cortex using fluorescent in situ hybdrization (FISH), with 97% of Chat+ neurons expressing Cre and 100% of Cre+ neurons expressing Chat (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data presented in Figure 1B showing quantification of co-labeling (n = 32 Chat+/Cre+ of 33 Chat+ and 32 Cre+ neurons from 2 Chatires-Cre mice).

claim: A population of neurons in the subiculum are strongly labeled in Chatires-Cre x Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice but do not express Chat in the adult.
source: In contrast, a population of neurons in the subiculum are also strongly labeled in Chatires-Cre x Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice (Figure 1A), but do not express Chat in the adult (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated explicitly but supporting data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The majority of cortical ChAT+ neurons express Slc18a3, the gene encoding VAChT.
source: Both of these genes are also expressed in the majority of cortical ChAT+ neurons (Figure 1C,D), indicating that cortical ChAT+ neurons have all the molecular machinery necessary to release ACh.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data in Figure 1C showing co-labeling of Chat and Slc18a3 (n = 147 Chat+/Slc18a3+ of 170 Chat+ and 184 Slc18a3+ neurons from 3 wild-type mice).

claim: The majority of cortical ChAT+ neurons express Slc5a7, the gene encoding the membrane choline transporter.
source: Both of these genes are also expressed in the majority of cortical ChAT+ neurons (Figure 1C,D), indicating that cortical ChAT+ neurons have all the molecular machinery necessary to release ACh.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data in Figure 1D showing co-labeling of Chat and Slc5a7 (n = 72 Chat+,Slc5a7+ of 113 Chat+ and 83 Slc5a7+ neurons from 3 wild-type mice).

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons have all the molecular machinery necessary to release ACh.
source: Both of these genes are also expressed in the majority of cortical ChAT+ neurons (Figure 1C,D), indicating that cortical ChAT+ neurons have all the molecular machinery necessary to release ACh.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression of Chat, Slc18a3, and Slc5a7 in cortical ChAT+ neurons.

claim: 66% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons display a bipolar morphology with two main vertical dendrites.
source: These neurons display a vertically-oriented morphology, with their main dendrites aligned perpendicular to the cortical surface, and are either bipolar, with two main vertical dendrites (Figure 1E, 66% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons) or multipolar, with three or more main dendrites (Figure 1E, 34% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1E and quantified in Figure 1F (n = 207 bipolar neurons, 66% of total).

claim: 34% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons display a multipolar morphology with three or more main dendrites.
source: These neurons display a vertically-oriented morphology, with their main dendrites aligned perpendicular to the cortical surface, and are either bipolar, with two main vertical dendrites (Figure 1E, 66% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons) or multipolar, with three or more main dendrites (Figure 1E, 34% of all cortical ChAT+ neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1E and quantified in Figure 1F (n = 107 multipolar neurons, 34% of total).

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons cluster in superficial layers, especially near the border between layers 1 and 2.
source: They cluster in superficial layers, especially near the border between layers 1 and 2 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by laminar distribution analysis in Figure 1F showing median cell body depth of 274 µm from pia (n = 1059 neurons from 3 mice).

claim: The median cortical ChAT+ neuron cell body is 274 µm from the pia.
source: Distribution of cortical depth from the pia of all cortical ChAT+ neurons (left graph, black trace, n = 1059 neurons from 3 Chatires-Cre x Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice), median cell body is 274 µm from pia ±15 µm, 95% C.I.)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar distribution shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons comprise an ~33% subset of VIP+ interneurons.
source: We confirmed using both immunohistochemistry and FISH that cortical ChAT+ neurons comprise an ~33% subset of VIP+ interneurons (Figure 2A,B), and do not co-label with either parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (Sst, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2A (n = 127 ChAT+/VIP+ neurons of 147 total ChAT+ and 375 VIP+ neurons from 3 mice) and FISH data in Figure 2B (n = 278 Chat+/Vip+ of 283 Chat+ and 579 Vip+ neurons from 3 mice).

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons do not co-label with parvalbumin (PV).
source: We confirmed using both immunohistochemistry and FISH that cortical ChAT+ neurons comprise an ~33% subset of VIP+ interneurons (Figure 2A,B), and do not co-label with either parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (Sst, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing n = 1 ChAT+,PV+ of 180 CHAT+ and 576 PV+ neurons from 3 mice.

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons do not co-label with somatostatin (Sst).
source: We confirmed using both immunohistochemistry and FISH that cortical ChAT+ neurons comprise an ~33% subset of VIP+ interneurons (Figure 2A,B), and do not co-label with either parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (Sst, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing n = 2 ChAT+/Sst+ of 360 ChAT+ and 1016 Sst+ neurons from 3 mice.

claim: Nearly all cortical ChAT+ neurons express Slc32a1, which encodes the vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT).
source: To test whether cortical ChAT+ neurons are able to release GABA, we performed FISH for the GABA handling and synthesis genes Slc32a1, encoding the vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT), and Gad1,2, which encode the GABA synthetic enzymes. Nearly all cortical ChAT+ neurons express both Slc32a1 and Gad1,2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data in Figure 2C showing n = 101 Chat+,Slc32a1+ of 102 Chat+ neurons from 5 mice.

claim: Nearly all cortical ChAT+ neurons express Gad1 and Gad2, which encode the GABA synthetic enzymes.
source: To test whether cortical ChAT+ neurons are able to release GABA, we performed FISH for the GABA handling and synthesis genes Slc32a1, encoding the vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT), and Gad1,2, which encode the GABA synthetic enzymes. Nearly all cortical ChAT+ neurons express both Slc32a1 and Gad1,2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data in Figure 2C showing n = 102 Chat+,Gad1/2+ of 102 Chat+ neurons from 5 mice.

claim: Cortical VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons have the potential for synaptic release of both ACh and GABA.
source: In sum, these data show that cortical VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons have the potential for synaptic release of both ACh and GABA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression of genes for both ACh and GABA synthesis and release machinery.

claim: A subset of Vip-expressing cortical interneurons also express cholinergic genes Chat, Slc5a7, Slc18a3, and GABAergic genes Slc32a1, Gad1, and Gad2, but not glutamatergic genes.
source: These results are corroborated by single-cell RNA sequencing data from the Allen Institute (Tasic et al., 2016), indicating that a subset of Vip-expressing cortical interneurons also express cholinergic genes Chat, Slc5a7, Slc18a3, and GABAergic genes Slc32a1, Gad1, and Gad2, but not glutamatergic genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data from Tasic et al., 2016, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most synaptic output from cortical VIP+/ChAT+ neurons is GABAergic.
source: A systematic survey of synaptic connectivity shows that, for these cells, most synaptic output is GABAergic.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3G.

claim: Of neurons that displayed a detectable synaptic response following optogenetic stimulation of cortical ChAT+ neurons, most showed a GABAAR-mediated current.
source: Of the neurons that displayed a detectable synaptic response following optogenetic stimulation of the cortical ChAT+ neurons, most showed a GABAAR-mediated current, confirming that cortical ChAT+ neurons are indeed GABAergic.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A smaller subset of neurons in superficial layers showed nAChR-mediated synaptic responses following optogenetic stimulation of cortical ChAT+ neurons.
source: A smaller subset of neurons in superficial layers showed nAChR-mediated synaptic responses (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All but two (of 49) responsive neurons displayed either GABAAR- or nAChR-mediated currents, not both.
source: All but two (of 49) responsive neurons displayed either GABAAR- or nAChR-mediated currents, not both, indicating that the synaptic release of GABA or ACh by cortical ChAT+ neurons is independent and differentially targeted based on the output neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity analysis.

claim: The synaptic release of GABA or ACh by cortical ChAT+ neurons is independent and differentially targeted based on the postsynaptic target neuron.
source: All but two (of 49) responsive neurons displayed either GABAAR- or nAChR-mediated currents, not both, indicating that the synaptic release of GABA or ACh by cortical ChAT+ neurons is independent and differentially targeted based on the output neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that postsynaptic neurons receive either GABA or ACh, but not both.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ neurons release GABA robustly onto Sst+ interneurons.
source: Specifically, GABA release is robust onto somatostatin (Sst)-expressing interneurons, similar to the larger population of VIP+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3G showing high connectivity to Sst+ interneurons.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ neurons release ACh sparsely and highly specifically, mostly onto layer 1 interneurons and other cortical VIP+/ChAT+ neurons.
source: However, these cells are capable of releasing ACh, with sparse and highly specific targeting of ACh mostly onto layer 1 interneurons and other cortical VIP+/ChAT+ neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3K.

claim: Two distinct populations of pre-synaptic terminals exist in VIP+/ChAT+ neurons: a subset that are competent to release both GABA and ACh and others that can only release GABA.
source: Target-specificity is partially specified at the pre-synaptic level, as we identified two distinct populations of pre-synaptic terminals: a subset that are competent to release both GABA and ACh and others that can only release GABA.
evidence: The claim is supported by array tomography and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: A sparse population of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons is found in the mPFC.
source: The second class of cortical ChAT+ interneurons is molecularly and functionally distinct from VIP+ cholinergic interneurons and was discovered in an effort to reconcile our results with those of another study that described predominantly ACh, and not GABA release, from cortical ChAT+ interneurons (Obermayer et al., 2019). This sparse population of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons is found in the mPFC, has a distinct developmental origin from VIP+ interneurons, and contributes primarily cholinergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and genetic labeling data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7C,D.

claim: Non-VIP ChAT+ neurons in the mPFC have a distinct developmental origin from VIP+ interneurons.
source: This sparse population of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons is found in the mPFC, has a distinct developmental origin from VIP+ interneurons, and contributes primarily cholinergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic lineage tracing data using Nkx2.1ires-Flp shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Non-VIP ChAT+ neurons in the mPFC contribute primarily cholinergic signaling.
source: This sparse population of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons is found in the mPFC, has a distinct developmental origin from VIP+ interneurons, and contributes primarily cholinergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The pattern of GABAergic connectivity from VIP+/ChAT+ neurons is consistent with previous analyses of VIP+ cells.
source: This pattern of connectivity is consistent with reports for VIP+ interneurons as a whole (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016a), and indicates that the main circuit function of cortical VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons is disinhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published literature (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016a).

claim: The main circuit function of cortical VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons is disinhibition.
source: This pattern of connectivity is consistent with reports for VIP+ interneurons as a whole (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016a), and indicates that the main circuit function of cortical VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons is disinhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of GABAergic connectivity onto inhibitory interneurons.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ neurons found high rates of GABAergic connectivity, especially onto Sst+ interneurons.
source: We found high rates of GABAergic connectivity, especially onto Sst+ interneurons, while nAChR-mediated responses were rare (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: nAChR-mediated responses from VIP+/ChAT+ neurons were rare.
source: We found high rates of GABAergic connectivity, especially onto Sst+ interneurons, while nAChR-mediated responses were rare (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GABA release from cortical ChAT+ cells is monosynaptic.
source: In each of these specific neuronal subtypes, we confirmed that GABA release from cortical ChAT+ cells was monosynaptic and confirmed that between these 4 interneuron classes, we spanned the entire cortical column (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TTX and 4AP experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A low overall rate of connectivity from VIP+/ChAT+ neurons to pyramidal neurons was observed, which was entirely GABAAR-mediated.
source: We also targeted pyramidal neurons based on their morphology and laminar position and found a low overall rate of connectivity, which was entirely GABAAR-mediated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 (n = 58 neurons from 14 mice).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of VIP+/ChAT+ neurons did not significantly affect pre-synaptic glutamate release.
source: Contrary to the findings of von Engelhardt et al., we did not observe any significant effect of optogenetic stimulation on pre-synaptic glutamate release (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by sEPSC frequency and amplitude measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 (n = 5 neurons from 2 mice).

claim: ACh release from VIP+ interneurons is not necessary for optogenetic- or sensory-evoked vasodilation.
source: Although we confirmed that optogenetic stimulation of VIP+ interneurons is sufficient to induce vasodilation, using a genetic strategy that eliminates Ach release from VIP+ interneurons, we found that ACh release from these cells is not necessary for optogenetic- or sensory-evoked vasodilation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 using Vipires-Cre x Slc18a3fl/fl mice.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ neurons largely release GABA onto each other.
source: We found that VIP+/ChAT+ neurons largely release GABA onto each other (Figure 3I,K), but that a subset received nAChR-input which could be blocked by nAChR-selective antagonists (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3I,K (n = 76 neurons from 8 mice).

claim: A subset of VIP+/ChAT+ neurons receive nAChR-input from other VIP+/ChAT+ neurons.
source: We found that VIP+/ChAT+ neurons largely release GABA onto each other (Figure 3I,K), but that a subset received nAChR-input which could be blocked by nAChR-selective antagonists (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: Both VGAT and VAChT are enriched within cortical ChAT+ interneuron terminals.
source: Across all samples, Synapsin-1, Gephyrin, VGAT, ChAT, and VAChT were consistently enriched within cortical ChAT+ interneuron terminals, whereas PSD-95 and VGLUT1 were specifically depleted (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by array tomography colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PSD-95 and VGLUT1 are specifically depleted from cortical ChAT+ interneuron terminals.
source: Across all samples, Synapsin-1, Gephyrin, VGAT, ChAT, and VAChT were consistently enriched within cortical ChAT+ interneuron terminals, whereas PSD-95 and VGLUT1 were specifically depleted (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by array tomography colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Individual cortical VIP+/ChAT+ terminals have highly variable expression of VAChT.
source: These data show that individual cortical VIP+/ChAT+ terminals have highly variable expression of VAChT (Figure 5B–D), with some axon stretches entirely lacking VAChT (Figure 5B), others being entirely positive for VAChT (Figure 5C), and some stretches presenting intermingled VAChT-containing and VAChT-lacking terminals (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Some axon stretches of VIP+/ChAT+ neurons are entirely lacking VAChT.
source: These data show that individual cortical VIP+/ChAT+ terminals have highly variable expression of VAChT (Figure 5B–D), with some axon stretches entirely lacking VAChT (Figure 5B), others being entirely positive for VAChT (Figure 5C), and some stretches presenting intermingled VAChT-containing and VAChT-lacking terminals (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Some axon stretches of VIP+/ChAT+ neurons are entirely positive for VAChT.
source: These data show that individual cortical VIP+/ChAT+ terminals have highly variable expression of VAChT (Figure 5B–D), with some axon stretches entirely lacking VAChT (Figure 5B), others being entirely positive for VAChT (Figure 5C), and some stretches presenting intermingled VAChT-containing and VAChT-lacking terminals (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Some axon stretches of VIP+/ChAT+ neurons present intermingled VAChT-containing and VAChT-lacking terminals.
source: These data show that individual cortical VIP+/ChAT+ terminals have highly variable expression of VAChT (Figure 5B–D), with some axon stretches entirely lacking VAChT (Figure 5B), others being entirely positive for VAChT (Figure 5C), and some stretches presenting intermingled VAChT-containing and VAChT-lacking terminals (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The majority of VIP+/ChAT+ terminals are positive for both VGAT and VAChT.
source: By this classification, the majority of terminals are positive for both VGAT and VAChT (Figure 5G, R2 = 0.232), with a subset that are positive for VGAT but not VAChT (Figure 5G, R2 = 0.091).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of terminal immunostaining shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A subset of VIP+/ChAT+ terminals are positive for VGAT but not VAChT.
source: By this classification, the majority of terminals are positive for both VGAT and VAChT (Figure 5G, R2 = 0.232), with a subset that are positive for VGAT but not VAChT (Figure 5G, R2 = 0.091).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of terminal immunostaining shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A significantly larger proportion of layer 1 neurons receives cholinergic input in the mPFC compared to M1.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that a significantly larger proportion of layer 1 neurons receives cholinergic input in the mPFC compared to in M1 (20/131 neurons with nAChR responses in mPFC compared to 1/43 in M1) and significantly fewer proportion of GABAergic responses (9/131 neurons with GABAAR responses compared to 13/43 in M1, Figure 6F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 6F-H (n = 174 neurons from 9 mice).

claim: A significantly smaller proportion of layer 1 neurons receives GABAergic input from local ChAT+ neurons in the mPFC compared to M1.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that a significantly larger proportion of layer 1 neurons receives cholinergic input in the mPFC compared to in M1 (20/131 neurons with nAChR responses in mPFC compared to 1/43 in M1) and significantly fewer proportion of GABAergic responses (9/131 neurons with GABAAR responses compared to 13/43 in M1, Figure 6F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Only a single cholinergic response was identified from VIP+ interneurons in mPFC and M1, with the majority of synaptic responses being GABAergic.
source: However, we only identified a single cholinergic response in mPFC, with the majority of synaptic responses from VIP+ interneuron activation in mPFC and M1 being GABAergic (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 6J-L (n = 64 neurons from 7 mice).

claim: Fluorescent in situ hybridization revealed a sparse population of neurons in the mPFC that express high levels of Chat but not Vip mRNA.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization for Chat and Vip revealed a sparse population of neurons in the mPFC that express high levels of Chat but not Vip mRNA (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Non-VIP ChAT+ neurons in the mPFC derive from Nkx2.1-expressing progenitors.
source: Indeed, using an intersectional genetic strategy (Plummer et al., 2015; He et al., 2016) to label neurons that express, even transiently, both Chat and Nkx2.1 (Chatires-Cre x Nkx2.1ires-Flp x RC:FLTG), we identified Nkx2.1-lineage neurons in the mPFC that immunolabel for ChAT but not for VIP (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7C,D using Chatires-Cre x Nkx2.1ires-Flp x RC:FLTG mice.

claim: Non-VIP ChAT+ neurons are exceptionally sparse, with only 3-5 neurons identifiable in each analyzed mouse brain.
source: These neurons were exceptionally sparse - both non-VIP, ChAT+ neurons identified by FISH (Figure 7B) and Nkx2.1+/ChAT+ neurons identified genetically (Figure 7C,D), only 3–5 neurons were identifiable in each analyzed mouse brain, indicating that these are the same population of cells (see additional examples of morphology and orientation in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of FISH and genetic labeling experiments.

claim: Layer 1 interneurons near ChR2-expressing non-VIP ChAT+ neurons received nicotinic cholinergic input following optogenetic stimulation, but not GABAergic synaptic currents.
source: Indeed, layer 1 interneurons near ChR2-expressing non-VIP ChAT+ neurons (but without nearby VIP+/ChAT+ neurons) received nicotinic cholinergic following optogenetic stimulation, but not GABAergic synaptic currents (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 7F (n = 30 neurons from 6 mice).

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons co-transmit both GABA and ACh, targeting each neurotransmitter onto different post-synaptic neurons.
source: In this study, we characterized the synaptic physiology and anatomy of cortical ChAT+ interneurons, focusing primarily on the vast majority that are a subset of VIP+ interneurons. These VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons co-transmit both GABA and ACh, targeting each neurotransmitter onto different post-synaptic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity and molecular data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ACh transmission from VIP+/ChAT+ neurons is sparse and primarily targets layer 1 interneurons and other VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons.
source: ACh transmission is sparse and primarily targets layer 1 interneurons and other VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figures 3D and 3K.

claim: GABA transmission from VIP+/ChAT+ neurons is widespread onto inhibitory interneuron subtypes, especially Sst+ interneurons.
source: In contrast, GABA transmission is widespread onto inhibitory interneuron subtypes, especially Sst+ interneurons, a pattern of GABAergic connectivity that is consistent with previous analyses of VIP+ cells (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Karnani et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological connectivity data shown in Figure 3G and comparison to published literature.

claim: The majority of VIP+/ChAT+ synapses are competent to release both ACh and GABA.
source: However, given the enrichment for ACh synthesis and release proteins in the pre-synaptic terminals and our finding that the majority of VIP+/ChAT+ synapses are competent to release both ACh and GABA, the relative sparsity of ACh-mediated responses remains surprising.
evidence: The claim is supported by array tomography and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: ACh-mediated excitation of layer 1 and VIP+/ChAT+ disinhibitory interneurons, combined with GABA-mediated disinhibition, provides a powerful activating signal to local cortical areas.
source: Nevertheless, the pattern of GABA and ACh connectivity we describe suggests a coherent model of the net effect that these neurons have on cortical circuits: ACh-mediated excitation of other layer 1 and VIP+/ChAT+ disinhibitory interneurons, combined with the GABA-mediated disinhibition, provides a powerful activating signal to local cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the connectivity data.

claim: Cortical ChAT+ neurons in barrel cortex are strongly activated by sensory stimuli.
source: Cortical ChAT+ neurons in barrel cortex are strongly activated by sensory stimuli, supporting this model, but optogenetic activation of cortical ChAT+ neurons actually slightly decreases the response of other neurons to whisker deflections (Dudai et al., 2020), suggesting additional complexities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dudai et al., 2020.

claim: Optogenetic activation of cortical ChAT+ neurons slightly decreases the response of other neurons to whisker deflections.
source: Cortical ChAT+ neurons in barrel cortex are strongly activated by sensory stimuli, supporting this model, but optogenetic activation of cortical ChAT+ neurons actually slightly decreases the response of other neurons to whisker deflections (Dudai et al., 2020), suggesting additional complexities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dudai et al., 2020.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons are a local source of ACh that is sparse and highly targeted, contrasting with the broadly dispersed, long-range projections from the basal forebrain.
source: First, they are a local source of ACh that is sparse and highly targeted, contrasting with the broadly dispersed, long-range projections from the basal forebrain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity data and comparison to known basal forebrain projections.

claim: VIP+/ChAT+ interneurons provide an example of specialized pre-synaptic terminals that allow for targeting of different neurotransmitters to specific outputs.
source: Second, they provide an example of specialized pre-synaptic terminals that allow for targeting of different neurotransmitters to specific outputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular and functional data showing differential expression of VAChT in terminals.

claim: Multiple levels of heterogeneity exist within cortical ChAT+ neurons.
source: Third, our study identifies a multiple levels of heterogeneity within cortical ChAT+ neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the identification of VIP+ and non-VIP ChAT+ neurons with different properties.

claim: Multiple subtypes of cortical ChAT+ neurons exist that differ in developmental origins, molecular profiles, and synaptic connectivity.
source: The first is existence of multiple subtypes of cortical ChAT+ neurons that differ in developmental origins, molecular profiles, and synaptic connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing VIP+ (CGE-derived) and non-VIP (MGE-derived) ChAT+ neurons.

claim: Non-VIP ChAT+ neurons are found only in the mPFC within cortex.
source: Notably, within cortex these non-VIP ChAT+ neurons are found only mPFC, potentially why they are not identifiable in recently published single-cell RNA sequencing data sets (Saunders et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2015) and have evaded widespread notice.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-brain survey data mentioned in the text.

claim: The presence of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons explains the differences in connectivity between this study and Obermayer et al., 2019.
source: The presence of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons explains the differences in connectivity between our study and a recent one that examind cortical ChAT+ interneuron connectivity in the mPFCanderroneously attributed all local cholinergic connectivity to VIP+/ChAT+ neurons (Obermayer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discovery of non-VIP ChAT+ neurons and comparison to Obermayer et al., 2019.

claim: Studies that use ChAT-BAC-ChR2 mice to activate cholinergic neurons run the risk of confounding gain-of-function effects due to overexpressed VAChT.
source: Studies that use ChAT-BAC-ChR2 mice to activate cholinergic neurons not only run the risk of confounding gain-of-function effects due to overexpressed VAChT (Kolisnyk et al., 2013), but also from incidental manipulation of cortical VIP+ interneurons, which are known to have profound effects on cortical function even purely through GABA release.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kolisnyk et al., 2013.

claim: Studies that use ChAT-BAC-ChR2 mice run the risk of confounding effects from incidental manipulation of cortical VIP+ interneurons.
source: Studies that use ChAT-BAC-ChR2 mice to activate cholinergic neurons not only run the risk of confounding gain-of-function effects due to overexpressed VAChT (Kolisnyk et al., 2013), but also from incidental manipulation of cortical VIP+ interneurons, which are known to have profound effects on cortical function even purely through GABA release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that cortical ChAT+ neurons are VIP+ interneurons.

claim: Studies of cholinergic signaling in cortex must differentiate between contributions from basal forebrain projections and those from local cholinergic interneurons.
source: Going forward, studies of cholinergic signaling in cortex must differentiate between contributions from basal forebrain projections and those from local cholinergic interneurons.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.
